title: Soft Skills Baseline Assessment
theme: Real-world decision making across 10 everyday scenarios
description: 10 real-world scenarios to measure how you naturally think, decide, and respond under pressure. No right or wrong — just honest choices. Takes about 15 minutes.
target_audience: Students, professionals, and anyone starting their Mento journey
learning_objectives: Establish your personal baseline across 8 key dimensions
Understand how you naturally respond under pressure
Identify your strongest dimensions and areas for growth
how_to_play: Read each scenario carefully and choose the response that feels most like what you would actually do — not what you think is the 'right' answer. Your honest choices create the most useful baseline.
psychological_framework: Situational judgment assessment based on behavioral decision theory

glossary_terms.definition: The process of choosing between different options after considering their consequences
Giving up one thing to gain another — every choice has a cost
A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term goal
The result or outcome of a choice or action
A particular way of looking at something — everyone has a different perspective

rounds.title: The Struggling Teammate
rounds.story: Your team has a major presentation in 48 hours. You've done your part. A teammate tells you they've barely started — they've been dealing with a family situation and are visibly stressed. The rest of the group hasn't noticed yet.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to your teammate's situation
rounds.coaching_moment: How you respond when someone else is struggling — especially when there's pressure on you too — reveals a great deal about how you balance empathy with responsibility.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time someone on your team was struggling. What did you actually do? What do you wish you'd done?

choices.label: Check in privately, understand what happened, and offer to help redistribute the work
choices.feedback: You made time to understand before acting. That private check-in prevents embarrassment, builds trust, and lets you make a clear-headed decision about how to move forward. This is how high-functioning teams handle pressure.
choices.coaching_moment: The best response to a struggling teammate is almost never public. A private, non-judgmental conversation creates the space for honesty.

choices.label: Tell the group in the next meeting so everyone can decide together how to handle it
choices.feedback: Transparency feels fair, but exposing someone's personal struggles in a group setting without their consent can damage trust and create defensiveness. The group can decide together — but only after the person has been spoken to privately.
choices.coaching_moment: Transparency and privacy aren't opposites. You can be open with the team while still protecting someone's dignity.

choices.label: Cover their work yourself without saying anything — you'd rather just get it done
choices.feedback: Doing the extra work shows commitment, but doing it silently stores resentment and doesn't help your teammate grow or take ownership. It also creates a pattern where others don't need to be accountable because you'll always absorb the cost.
choices.coaching_moment: Absorbing others' work without acknowledgment is generous in the short term but unsustainable. The sustainable move is to address the gap, not hide it.

rounds.image_prompt: teammates in an office, one looking stressed at their laptop, another approaching with concern
rounds.scene_hint: modern open-plan office, late afternoon, tension and care in the air

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Career Crossroads
rounds.story: You're offered two jobs: a stable role at a well-known company at ₹8 LPA with predictable growth, and a founding team role at an early-stage startup at ₹5 LPA with meaningful equity. The startup is working on something you genuinely believe in. You have no financial dependents.
rounds.goal: Choose the career path that reflects your thinking
rounds.coaching_moment: How you weigh certainty against potential reveals your relationship with risk and your ability to think long-term — two dimensions that predict a great deal about how people perform under uncertainty.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you imagine yourself 5 years from now — what matters more to you: stability or ownership?

choices.label: Take the stable job — financial security now lets you think clearly about the future
choices.feedback: Choosing security is rational, especially with real financial obligations. Without those, it signals risk aversion. The reasoning here matters — if you chose stability because you genuinely want to optimize for learning and later impact, that's strategic. If it's fear, that's worth examining.
choices.coaching_moment: Risk aversion isn't a flaw — but being aware of whether your choices are driven by strategy or fear is one of the most valuable things you can know about yourself.

choices.label: Take the startup role — the potential upside and belief in the mission outweigh the salary cut
choices.feedback: With no financial dependents and genuine belief in the mission, taking calculated risk on asymmetric upside is rational — not reckless. This choice reflects comfort with uncertainty, long-term thinking, and the ability to act on conviction without needing certainty.
choices.coaching_moment: The expected value of a decision includes not just salary but learning rate, equity, and how much you'll care about showing up. The startup role scores high on all three.

choices.label: Negotiate hard at the stable company to get a higher salary, then decide
choices.feedback: Using one offer to negotiate better terms at another is good strategy. This approach shows you understand leverage — but if you ultimately take the stable job after negotiating, you're still signaling risk aversion. The negotiation itself is valuable practice regardless.
choices.coaching_moment: Negotiating is almost always worth doing. The outcome of the negotiation is a data point — what you choose afterward tells you more about your values.

rounds.image_prompt: young professional at a crossroads, two doors labeled 'stability' and 'startup', city skyline
rounds.scene_hint: thoughtful moment, career decision, two paths

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: The Honest Mistake
rounds.story: While reviewing your work, you realize you made a calculation error three days ago that slightly inflated a report your manager presented to the leadership team. No one has caught it. The number was off by about 8% — not catastrophic, but noticeable if scrutinized.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the error you discovered
rounds.coaching_moment: How someone behaves when no one is watching — especially when there's something to lose — is one of the best predictors of long-term trustworthiness and character.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a mistake you covered up or stayed quiet about. What happened? What did it cost you internally?

choices.label: Tell your manager immediately, explain what happened, and offer a corrected version
choices.feedback: Flagging your own error before anyone else does is one of the most trust-building things you can do. It demonstrates integrity, self-awareness, and the kind of reliability that builds long-term credibility. The discomfort is temporary; the trust you earn is durable.
choices.coaching_moment: The cost of honesty about a mistake is almost always lower than the cost of someone else finding it — and far lower than the cost of carrying the weight of knowing.

choices.label: Fix the document quietly and update the numbers without mentioning the original error
choices.feedback: Fixing quietly removes the problem from the document but not from the relationship. If someone later cross-references the original, you now have a much harder conversation ahead. The attempt to protect yourself creates a larger risk than the mistake itself did.
choices.coaching_moment: Quiet fixes feel like damage control but they're actually risk accumulation. You've added a layer of concealment to the original error.

choices.label: Wait and see — if no one notices, there's no need to create unnecessary anxiety
choices.feedback: Waiting and hoping something goes unnoticed is a passive choice that usually creates more anxiety than acting would. The decision to say nothing is still a decision — and it makes you responsible not just for the original error but for the concealment.
choices.coaching_moment: Every moment you wait to flag an error, you're adding a cost to what disclosure will eventually look like. Early honesty is almost always cheaper than late honesty.

rounds.image_prompt: person discovering an error in their report, looking at a computer screen with concern, empty office
rounds.scene_hint: quiet office, moment of ethical reckoning, fluorescent light

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Rejection
rounds.story: You prepared for 4 months for a national-level competition — research, coaching, mock rounds. You didn't make it past the preliminary stage. Three of your close friends who prepared alongside you did advance. You have two weeks before the next round you're eligible for.
rounds.goal: Choose how you respond to not advancing
rounds.coaching_moment: Setbacks are the most reliable test of resilience. The quality of your response — not the failure itself — determines what happens next.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Recall a significant rejection or failure. What was your first instinct? What did you do 2 weeks later?

choices.label: Take a week off to decompress, then systematically analyze the feedback and plan what to fix
choices.feedback: Taking a brief recovery period before analyzing is emotionally intelligent — processing the loss before trying to learn from it prevents defensive rationalization. Coming back with a systematic plan shows that the setback made you more precise, not less motivated.
choices.coaching_moment: High performers don't skip the emotional processing — they do it quickly and deliberately. Grief is not the opposite of growth; unprocessed grief is.

choices.label: Jump immediately into preparing for the next competition without dwelling on this one
choices.feedback: Moving fast signals grit, but skipping the analysis means you're likely to repeat the same errors. The competitors who improve fastest aren't those who move on quickest — they're those who extract the most learning before moving on.
choices.coaching_moment: Speed is not the same as progress. A week of honest self-analysis is worth more than a month of practice built on incorrect assumptions about what went wrong.

choices.label: Take an extended break and reconsider whether to continue competing at all
choices.feedback: One setback after significant preparation is not a reliable signal to quit — it's a signal to refine. Reconsidering the whole endeavor after a single loss conflates disappointment with evidence. This pattern, repeated, accumulates into a portfolio of abandoned goals.
choices.coaching_moment: The question is not whether to continue — it's whether your analysis of what went wrong is accurate. Quitting is a valid choice when based on information, not when based on feelings fresh from a loss.

rounds.image_prompt: young person sitting alone after a competition, friends celebrating in background, processing emotions
rounds.scene_hint: competition hall, contrast between defeat and celebration, growth moment

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Last-Minute Pivot
rounds.story: You're 20 hours from submitting a project you've spent 3 weeks building. Your manager calls and tells you the direction has changed — the client wants a completely different deliverable. The new ask is feasible but completely different from what you've built. Your existing work will not be used.
rounds.goal: Decide how to approach the change
rounds.coaching_moment: How you respond to sudden, unfair-feeling change — especially after significant investment — measures your adaptability and your ability to separate your emotional attachment from the practical problem.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When was the last time your effort was wasted through no fault of your own? How long did it take you to move forward?

choices.label: Accept the change, immediately triage the new deliverable, and focus on the highest-impact elements given the time
choices.feedback: This response — accepting what can't be changed and immediately redirecting energy toward the new problem — is the hallmark of high-performing people in fast-changing environments. You didn't waste time on blame or mourning the old work. You pivoted cleanly.
choices.coaching_moment: Sunk cost is real, but it is irrelevant to the decision at hand. The only useful question now is: given what you have, what can you build in 20 hours that will genuinely deliver value?

choices.label: Push back firmly — this is too late a change and someone needs to own the poor planning
choices.feedback: The frustration is valid — this was poor planning. But expressing it in the moment, when the deadline is 20 hours away, doesn't change the situation. It consumes time and political capital that would be better spent on the new deliverable. The right moment for this conversation is after delivery.
choices.coaching_moment: There is a time to push back on poor process and a time to absorb it and deliver. Reading which situation you're in — and acting accordingly — is a core professional skill.

choices.label: Ask for a 48-hour extension to do the new work properly rather than rushing
choices.feedback: Asking for more time rather than rushing is often the right call — it shows you respect quality over optics. Whether the extension is granted depends on context, but the willingness to have that conversation rather than silently deliver subpar work is mature.
choices.coaching_moment: The best professionals know the difference between a deadline that is truly fixed and one that only feels fixed. Asking for an extension, done correctly, is not weakness — it's precision.

rounds.image_prompt: professional on phone looking at discarded work and blank whiteboard with 20 hours left
rounds.scene_hint: urgent pivot, office chaos, clock on wall

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: The Quick Win vs. The Big Play
rounds.story: You have a free afternoon. You could finish a small, straightforward report that will be noticed and appreciated immediately — or you could spend the same time on a complex problem that no one has asked you to solve but that you think could significantly improve how your team operates. The complex problem might go nowhere.
rounds.goal: Choose how to use your unstructured time
rounds.coaching_moment: Choosing between immediate visible reward and uncertain long-term impact is one of the most recurring decisions in any professional life. What you choose here, repeated over years, determines whether you're seen as reliable or visionary — or both.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What's a problem in your environment that no one has asked you to solve but that you keep thinking about?

choices.label: Finish the quick report — delivering consistently on what's expected is how trust is built
choices.feedback: Consistent delivery is genuinely valuable — it builds credibility. But choosing the safe, visible task every time it's available is a pattern that makes you reliable but not indispensable. The most impactful professionals find the complex problems and solve them before being asked.
choices.coaching_moment: Reliability is table stakes. The real differentiation is finding the problems no one assigned and making them go away.

choices.label: Tackle the complex problem — if it works, the impact far exceeds the quick report
choices.feedback: Investing time in an unassigned problem with uncertain outcome is how leverage gets created. It might not work — but the practice of identifying high-value problems and working on them without being asked is what separates people who grow from people who stagnate.
choices.coaching_moment: The expected value of working on a big uncertain problem is often higher than a small certain one — especially when you have no competing obligations.

choices.label: Spend 30 minutes on the quick report, then use the rest of the time on the complex problem
choices.feedback: Splitting the time is pragmatic — you deliver on what's expected while creating space for initiative. This is often the optimal balance: don't abandon the basics, but don't let them crowd out everything else.
choices.coaching_moment: The ability to do both — meet expectations and go beyond them — without letting either cancel out the other is a genuine skill in time and energy management.

rounds.image_prompt: split scene: one person completing routine report vs another exploring a creative problem on a whiteboard
rounds.scene_hint: productive afternoon, choice between safe and ambitious

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: The Unfair Advantage
rounds.story: A close friend offers to share detailed notes from a past entrance exam that is widely known to reuse questions. Using the notes is technically not prohibited by any written rule, but it's clearly against the spirit of the assessment. The advantage would be significant.
rounds.goal: Decide whether and how to use the notes
rounds.coaching_moment: The clearest tests of ethical reasoning are the ones where the rules don't explicitly cover the situation — where you have to decide what you actually believe, not what you're required to do.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Where in your life do you follow the letter of a rule but not its spirit? Is that a problem?

choices.label: Decline — if the exam is meant to test knowledge, using past papers defeats the purpose and corrupts the signal
choices.feedback: This choice reflects a clear, internally consistent ethical framework: assessments are meant to generate accurate signals, and corrupting those signals — even when allowed by technicality — undermines the system's purpose. This kind of reasoning is rare and valuable.
choices.coaching_moment: The strongest ethical positions don't need external enforcement — they're based on first-principles reasoning about what is actually good, not just what is technically permitted.

choices.label: Use them — the exam design is flawed if it reuses questions, and you're playing the game as it is, not as it should be
choices.feedback: This is a pragmatically defensible position but a morally weak one. 'Everyone does it' and 'the system is flawed' are the two oldest rationalisations for self-serving behaviour. The system being imperfect doesn't automatically make exploiting its imperfections ethical.
choices.coaching_moment: Situational ethics — behaving ethically only when the system enforces it — is a liability in high-trust roles. The question is not what you can do; it's what you're willing to be.

choices.label: Use them as context to understand what topics are important, but don't memorize specific answers
choices.feedback: The line between 'understanding important topics' and 'preparing from past papers' is thinner than it appears. This middle path sounds reasonable but often functions as permission-granting for something closer to option B. If the exam reuses questions, using past papers prepares you for the exact thing being tested, regardless of intent.
choices.coaching_moment: When you have to construct elaborate distinctions to make a choice feel acceptable, that's usually a signal the choice itself is uncomfortable for a reason.

rounds.image_prompt: person holding exam study materials, looking thoughtful about ethical choice
rounds.scene_hint: quiet study room, ethical dilemma, moral weight

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Unconventional Idea
rounds.story: Your team has used the same process for three years. It works — outcomes are acceptable. You've identified an approach that, based on your research, could cut the work by 40% and improve quality. It requires learning a new tool and a temporary dip in output. You're not in a senior role.
rounds.goal: Decide whether and how to raise the new approach
rounds.coaching_moment: The decision to speak up with an unconventional idea — and how you do it — measures initiative, risk tolerance, and social intelligence simultaneously.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time you had an idea that would disrupt how things were done. Did you share it? What happened?

choices.label: Test the new approach on your own work first, then bring data to a one-on-one with your manager
choices.feedback: Testing first and bringing data is the highest-quality version of this move. You're not asking anyone to take a risk on your intuition — you're showing them results. This approach maximises the chance of adoption while minimising the risk to you and your team.
choices.coaching_moment: The best argument for a new idea is evidence. When you can show even a small experiment that confirms your hypothesis, you convert a pitch into a proof.

choices.label: Raise it openly in the next team meeting — transparency is better than a private pitch
choices.feedback: Open proposal is honest and shows confidence, but without data, you're asking senior colleagues to bet on your intuition in a group setting — which often triggers defensiveness from those who built the current process. The idea might be excellent but the forum might not be.
choices.coaching_moment: The best idea in the wrong forum often fails. Understanding which conversations to have in public and which to have in private is as important as having good ideas.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself — you're not senior enough to be proposing process changes and it might backfire
choices.feedback: This choice conflates hierarchy with permission. The most valuable contributors in any organisation raise ideas regardless of seniority — they just do it thoughtfully. Staying quiet to avoid risk is a pattern that compounds: the more often you don't speak, the less you have to say.
choices.coaching_moment: The question is not whether you're senior enough to have ideas — you're never too junior for that. The question is how to raise them in a way that creates traction rather than friction.

rounds.image_prompt: junior employee cautiously raising hand in meeting while showing data on laptop to manager
rounds.scene_hint: team meeting room, innovation meeting, nervous but determined

expert_pick.reason: Creative problem-solving is rated the #1 skill employers look for in future leaders.

rounds.title: The Invisible Contributor
rounds.story: Your junior colleague did the majority of the analytical work on a project that just received strong praise from senior leadership. The presentation was yours, and only your name was in the room. Your colleague knows they contributed but hasn't said anything. Leadership only knows your name.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the credit for this work
rounds.coaching_moment: How people handle the allocation of credit — especially when they could personally benefit from taking it — is one of the clearest signals of character and long-term leadership potential.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever had your contribution go unrecognized? How did it feel? What did it do to your motivation?

choices.label: Explicitly attribute the work in the next relevant conversation — 'The analysis was done by [colleague], I want to make sure that's on record'
choices.feedback: Proactively attributing credit — especially when no one is requiring you to — is one of the most powerful signals of character and leadership potential. It costs you almost nothing immediately and builds enormous trust with your team and with leadership over time.
choices.coaching_moment: The leaders people trust most are those who give credit down and absorb blame up. This one behaviour, repeated consistently, compounds into a reputation that no amount of self-promotion can buy.

choices.label: Mention both contributions in passing if it comes up naturally, but don't make a point of raising it
choices.feedback: Waiting for a natural moment to mention contributions is better than silence, but it's passive. Your colleague's contribution was not passive — they did the work. A passive acknowledgment doesn't match the size of the debt. The conversation needs to happen proactively.
choices.coaching_moment: Passivity in attribution is its own kind of taking. If you benefit from someone's work and don't actively correct the record, the silence functions as endorsement of the misattribution.

choices.label: Accept the recognition — you led the project and framing the work to leadership is a real skill that deserves credit
choices.feedback: This is a rationalisation. Framing and presenting are real skills — but they don't justify claiming analytical work you didn't do. The short-term gain in status comes at the cost of a colleague's trust and your own integrity. These costs appear slowly but are paid fully.
choices.coaching_moment: The most common self-deception in credit-taking is believing that contribution at any stage justifies claiming the full result. It doesn't. Attribution should be proportional and accurate.

rounds.image_prompt: professional acknowledging colleague in front of leadership, pointing to them with pride
rounds.scene_hint: boardroom, credit given generously, colleague's surprised grateful expression

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The High-Stakes Blank
rounds.story: You're midway through an important interview for a role you genuinely want. The interviewer asks a highly specific technical question that you genuinely don't know the answer to. This is not a case of nerves — you actually don't have this knowledge. The interviewer is watching closely.
rounds.goal: Choose how to respond to the question you can't answer
rounds.coaching_moment: How someone handles a moment of genuine not-knowing — in a high-stakes setting — measures resilience, self-awareness, and strategic communication simultaneously.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When have you been caught not knowing something important? What did you do? What do you wish you had done?

choices.label: Acknowledge you don't know, explain how you would go about finding the answer, and show your reasoning process
choices.feedback: This is the highest-quality response available. Interviewers who ask difficult questions often care more about how you think than whether you know — and demonstrating that you can reason through gaps, stay composed, and show intellectual honesty is more valuable than a lucky guess.
choices.coaching_moment: The willingness to say 'I don't know, and here's how I'd find out' is a much stronger signal than a wrong answer delivered with confidence. Intellectual honesty under pressure is rare and prized.

choices.label: Give your best guess confidently — showing confidence matters as much as accuracy
choices.feedback: Confidence is valuable, but confidence detached from competence is a liability. Interviewers with expertise will recognize a wrong answer immediately, and confidently delivered wrong answers signal worse judgment than honest uncertainty. The short-term comfort of sounding sure destroys the signal you're trying to send.
choices.coaching_moment: Confidence should be a wrapper around substance, not a substitute for it. The most credible people are confident about what they know and clear about what they don't.

choices.label: Redirect to a related area where you do have expertise — pivot smoothly and show what you know
choices.feedback: A smooth pivot shows verbal intelligence and the ability to reframe. But skilled interviewers notice pivots, and if they need the specific answer, the redirect creates a worse impression than honesty. This is a good second option — better than a wrong guess, not as good as direct acknowledgment.
choices.coaching_moment: Redirects work when the pivot is genuinely relevant and valuable. When they're clearly evasive, they signal that you know you don't know — which is worse than just saying it directly.

rounds.image_prompt: job candidate in interview, composing themselves thoughtfully before answering a hard question
rounds.scene_hint: interview room, professional confidence under pressure, thinking pose

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

achievements.title: Baseline Established
achievements.description: Completed your Soft Skills Baseline Assessment

transfer_exercises: This week, notice one moment where you had to choose between the easy/visible action and the harder/more impactful one. What did you choose?
Find one situation where you can give credit to someone else proactively — before being asked to.
Identify one process in your environment that no one is fixing. Spend 30 minutes thinking about how you would approach it differently.
target_age: Students, professionals, and anyone starting their Mento journey
cultural_context: Scenario-based decision-making develops the judgment and soft skills that India's employers consistently rank as their top hiring priorities. Soft Skills Baseline Assessment provides the realistic, consequence-driven practice that traditional education rarely offers.
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Soft Skills Baseline Assessment Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of Soft Skills Baseline Assessment. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
